【16】On follow-up examination two years later， the patient was well and taking thyroxin. Follow-up CT scans of the chest and ab-domen showed no evidence of recurrent or metastatic disease.

【17】DISCUSSION

【18】Renal cell carcinoma is most common in patients over 40years of age； with the peak incidence in 6 or 7h decade of life . It is most common in males， with a male-to-female ratio of 3：2. The tuor tends to metastasize widely， invading the veins and growing along the blood vessels. Metastases to the head and neck occur in 5-15% of cases .

【19】The most common sites of metastases in the head are the sine-nasal tract， skin， cervical lymph nodes， and mandible. Lingual metastases are rare. Forty-three cases oflingual me-tastasis have been reported； Table l  illustrates the report-ed cases of renal cell carcinoma metastasizing to tongue. 20of these were diagnosed during autopsy studies . Table 2 illustrates cases of renal cell carcinoma with lingual me-tastasis as initial presentation. Usually the base of the tongue is involved， perhaps owing to its rich vascular supply. Clear-cell tumors of the tongue present a diagnostic challenge be-cause of the difficulty in differentiating from clear-cell ma-lignancy of a salivary gland on microscopic examination. In our case， the microscopic features included closely packed cells with clear cytoplasm and pleomorphic nuclei， as well as a high degree of vascularity. Immunohistochemical stud-ies demonstrated positive staining for glycogen， vimentin， cytokeratin and Epithelial Membrane Antigen， as well as negative staining for Carcino Embryonic Antigen and S100.

【20】Many authors have suggested that radiotherapy provides the best form of palliation for lingual metastases secondary to renal cell carcinomas， even though these tumors usually are radio-resistant . Disappearance of lingual metastatic renal cell carcinoma after treatment with interferon alpha has also been reported . Surgery is an option when the tongue is the only site of metastasis or when， as in our case， the lesion is solitary， peripherally located， and easily resect-able . The reported prognosis for patients with a lingual metastasis from renal cell carcinoma is poor； the mean inter-val between diagnosis and death is 5 months. However， our patient remains disease free more than 2 years after surgery.

【21】Based on autopsy studies， the incidence of metastases to the thyroid varies from 2.9-24.5%. In a study that includ-ed more than 20，000 thyroidectomies over 20 years， Czech et al. found 12 cases of metastases in the thyroid， of which5 were from renal cell carcinomas . In their study of20，362 thyroidectomies done over 23 years， Wychulis et al， found that 5 of 10 thyroid metastases were from renal cell carcinoma . Metastatic cancer in the thyroid is rarely recognized clinically and may be observed years after the excision of primary tumor. In 13 of the 43 cases， which were published in English literature， this period was mentioned to be 10 years or longer.

【22】The treatment of metastatic renal cell carcinoma is contro-versial，principally because 30-40% of patients have metasta-ses when these carcinomas are first diagnosed， while 30-50%develop systemic tumor dissemination even after those car-cinomas have been surgically removed .

【23】CONCLUSIONS

【24】Lingual and thyroid metastases in the same patient from clear cell renal carcinoma， has not been reported in the lit-erature. Our experience with the case reported here em-phasizes the need for an aggressive surgical approach to both the original tumor and the metastases. Complete sur-gical resection of synchronous and metachronous meta-static lesions may be possible and provide effective therapy.

【0】ABSTRACT Apert syndrome is an autosomal dominant inherited condition characterised by craniosynostosis， syndactyly， mid-face hypoplasia， organ malformations， and mental retardation. As it is rarely encountered， there is little knowledge of the anaesthesia practice in the literature for this syndrome， and we present our experience of two cases undergoing bilateral syndactyly release under general anaesthesia.

【1】KEYWORDS Apert Syndrome， acrocephalosyndactyly， difficult airway

【2】Introduction

【3】Wheaton described Apert syndrome in 1894. In 1906， Dr Eu-gene Charles Apert published a summary of nine cases . It is a rare autosomal dominant disorder， with a frequency of1 in 100，000- 160，000 . Apert syndrome， also called acro-cephalosyndactyly， typically has craniosynostosis， midface hy-poplasia， and syndactyly. It poses an anaesthetic challenge be-cause of the difficulties related to airway management， intra-venous access， associated systemic anomalies (cardiac defects， polycystic kidneys & pyloric stenosis)  & increased incidence of bronchospasm & wheezing . We present anaesthetic con-cerns and management of a few cases of Apert syndrome，re-ferred to us for syndactyly release.

【4】Case 1

【5】A three-year-old male child with a body weight of 12 kg was admitted to our hospital for scheduled bilateral hand acro syn-dactyly release and full-thickness skin graft. This child had craniosynostosis， midfacial hypoplasia， orbital proptosis， and fusion of multiple digits in all limbs .

【6】Medical history， clinical examination， and investigations dur-ing pre-anaesthetic check-ups excluded any other coexisting malformations. The patient was delivered vaginally， and the parent gave us a history of NICU admission for 8 days after birth due to a feeding problem. All blood investigations showed normal results with haemoglobin 11.1 gm/dl. After informed parental consent， the child was scheduled for elective surgery under general anaesthesia. An intravenous 24G cannula was secured with difficulty in the left lower limb in the operation theatre.ECG does routine monitoring for heart rate， and blood pressure cuff was placed in an operated limb. An oxygen satura-tion probe was placed in his ear lobe as it's placement was diffi-cult due to syndactyly. Premedication was given with 5ugm/kg glycopyrrolate and 2ugm/kg fentanyl. General anaesthesia was induced with 2mg/kg Propofol &0.1mg/kg Vecuronium. An airway was placed during mask ventilation as there was some difficulty in ventilation due to facial deformity. After achieving full relaxation， tracheal intubation was done with an un-cuffed endotracheal tube size 4.5mm under direct laryngoscopy and confirmed by auscultation and ETCO2 (capnography). Anaes-thesia was maintained with Sevoflurane (0.5-1MAC) and N2O& oxygen in a 1：1 ratio and intermittent muscle relaxation with vecuronium. Eyes were covered with wet gauge pieces and artificial teardrops were applied properly to avoid injury due to proptosis. OT's room AC temperature was maintained at24 degrees， and a temperature probe was placed to monitor his body temperature. An intravenous paracetamol infusion of 14mg/kg was given for analgesia， along with fentanyl. In-jection of ketorolac was avoided as this kind of patient is very prone to bronchospasm. Intravenous fluid was maintained with Ringer's lactate solution in a paediatric drip set. The tourniquet time was monitored as it was placed on the operating limb. The operation was completed in 2 hours. The patient was reversed uneventfully with a combination of injection neostigmine and glycopyrrolate and sent to the recovery room.

【7】Case 2

【8】Our second patient， a female aged 9 months， delivered by nor-mal vaginal delivery， had no history of NICU admission after birth. She had brachycephaly， mid-face hypoplasia involving the maxilla， syndactyly in all four limbs .

【9】Pre-operative investigation findings were normal except for echocardiography which showed an atrial septal defect. Af-ter obtaining informed consent and 6 hours of fasting， an in-travenous injection of glycopyrrolate 5ugm/kg and fentanyl2ugm/kg was given for premedication after securing a 24 G can-nula in the left forearm. Care was taken to avoid air entry in the intravenous line as the child had ASD. Non-invasive blood pres-sure， ECG and SpO2 were monitored. After pre-oxygenation for 3 minutes， induction was done with 2mg/kg Propofol &0.1mg/kg vecuronium， and an uncuffed endotracheal tube size4.0mm was placed securely. Maintenance was performed with sevoflurane in nitrous oxide/oxygen (2：1) to avoid more left-to-right shunting of blood and intermittent injection of vecuronium. During anaesthesia， there was wheezing managed with nebulisa-tion and tube suctioning. Recovery， which was uneventful， was done with injection of neostigmine and glycopyrrolate. After extubation， the patient was given oxygen via mask @ 4L/ml as her Spo2 was 95% which returned to normal after 30 minutes in the recovery room.

【10】Discussion

【11】Apert syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused due to the mutation of fibroblast growth factor recptor-2 (FGFR-2) on chromosome 10q . Although generally paternal mutations are seen， most cases are sporadic and develop because of new mutations . In both cases， there was no family history of a similar disease. Syndactyly or webbing of fingers causes immo-bility of fingers due to ossification of interphalangeal joints due to segmentation of embryonic phalanges. A similar deformity can involve the foot (mitten hand and sock foot) . In addition， proper placement of the oxygen saturation probe can be an issue due to syndactyly.

【12】Significant challenges come to us due to difficult airways as there are airway problems like cervical vertebra fusion， ob-structive sleep apnea due to nasopharyngeal airway stenosis and tracheal stenosis . They also have associated anoma-lies like cardiac defects， polycystic kidneys & pyloric stenosis. So thorough preoperative evaluation should be done to iden- tify these issues. In our cases， we encountered difficulties in cannulation， positioning of oxygen saturation probe， face mask ventilation and bronchospasm， possibly due to increased airway secretions . We prepared laryngeal masks and emergency tracheostomy sets for our cases， although neither was needed. In our second case， which had ASD， precaution was taken to avoid air embolism and increase in left to right shunt. Our first case had proptosis， so care was taken to cover his eyes with a wet gauge and proper lubrication.

【13】Due to various abnormalities， Apert Syndrome cases are can-didates for frequent surgeries and anaesthesia in multiple set-tings. Due to abnormal airways， difficult ventilation， intubation and respiratory complications are expected during anaesthesia. For safe anaesthesia management of these patients， comprehen-sive evaluation and preparations for possible complications are required.

【14】Conclusion

【15】In Apert syndrome， the anaesthetist must be ready for airway problems， intubation difficulties and visceral anomalies related to anaesthetic challenges. Thorough preoperative evaluation and proper perioperative alertness and management are key to success.

【0】Background：

【1】Granulocytic sarcoma， or 'chloroma，' due to extramedullary acute myeloid leukemia (AML) or due to acute my-elomonocytic leukemia (AML M5)， is rare and is associated with a poor prognosis. This report is of a case of granulocytic sarcoma of the gallbladder and describes the approach to diagnosis and treatment.

【2】Case Report：

【3】A 74-year-old Hispanic woman from Ecuador presented to the emergency department with a five-day history of fever， jaundice， and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. The right upper quadrant ultrasound showed a thickened gallbladder wall with cholelithiasis， a positive sonographic Murphy sign， and marked dilatation of the common bile duct， which was up to 17 mm in diameter. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography(ERCP) showed purulence and a stone in the common bile duct， which was removed. She underwent laparo-scopic cholecystectomy which identified gangrenous cholecystitis. Despite cholecystectomy and treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics， she remained febrile with a leukocytosis of up to 80，000 cells/uL Histopathology of the gallbladder showed infiltrating myeloblasts within the mucosa， submucosa， and muscularis consistent with a granulocytic sarcoma associated with gangrenous cholecystitis due to cholelithiasis.Immunohistochemistry using a panel of antibodies to CD33， CD68，HLA-DR， and lysozyme， supported the diagnosis of granulocytic sar- coma or extramedullary acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML M5).

【4】Conclusions：

【5】A rare case of an extramedullary hematologic malignancy granulocytic sarcoma of the gallbladder is presented， which highlights the importance of timely diagnosis and treatment， due to the high mortality rate associated with granulocytic sarcoma， or extramedullary AML.

【6】MeSH Keywords： Hematologic Neoplasms· Leukemia， Myeloid， Acute·Sarcoma， Myeloid

【7】Granulocytic sarcoma， or extramedullary acute myeloid leukemia (AML)， or chloroma， is rare and is associated with a poor prognosis. Granulocytic sarcoma is associated with a worse prognosis than AML The French-American-British (FAB) hematologic disease classification system classifies acute my elomonocytic leukemia as AML M5.

【8】We present an unusually rare case of a 74-year-old woman who presented initially with hepatobiliary sepsis and who was subsequently diagnosed with a primary granulocytic sarcoma of the gallbladder.

【9】Case Report

【10】A 74-year-old Hispanic woman from Ecuador with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency depart-ment with a five-day history of fever， jaundice， and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She traveled to America from Ecuador five days prior to hospital admission after several months of unintentional weight loss. Her abdominal pain was diffuse， but was most prominent in the right upper quadrant and epigastric region， and was associated with vomiting that did not con-tain blood or bile. The patient denied symptoms of chest pain， dyspnea， melena， hematochezia， dysuria， and hematuria. She had no history of cigarette， alcohol， or substance abuse， and no family history of cancer In the emergency department， she was found to have a markedly an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 800 IU/L， serum creatinine of 3.83 mg/dL， an international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.4， and serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of471 U/L. A complete blood count (CBC) showed leukocytosis with a predominant monocytosis (17，300 cells/pL)， marked thrombocytopenia (10，000/pL)， and macrocytic anemia that in-cluded hemoglobin (Hb) 9 g/dL， and a mean corpuscular volume(MCV) of 102.4 fL， and no blasts were identified. Because a di-agnosis of sepsis was made， she was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

【11】Ultrasound imaging of the right upper quadrant showed cho-lelithiasis and a thickened gallbladder wall with a positive so-nographic Murphy sign， or abdominal tenderness during pres-sure from the ultrasound probe. The common bile duct was dilated， measuring up to 17 mm in diameter. Endoscopic ret-rograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) showed purulence and a stone in the common bile duct， which was removed. A sphincterotomy was not performed due to the presence of thrombocytopenia. However， a plastic stent was placed in the common bile duct.

【12】Due to progressive leukocytosis and continued fevers， she un-derwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy with the insertion of a Jackson-Pratt drain， which was done without complications. Intraoperatively， the gallbladder appeared gangrenous. She was given 1.8 liters of crystalloid fluid， two units of platelets， and one unit of irradiated packed red blood cells (PRBCs) during surgery. Despite cholecystectomy and the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics，she continued to have a fever and pro-gressive leukocytosis of up to 80，000 cells/pL. Her condition deteriorated， with a clinical appearance of sepsis. At the re quest of her family， active treatment was discontinued， and she was made as comfortable as possible.

【13】Histopathology of the gallbladder showed myeloblasts， promy-elocytes， and myelocytes within the mucosa， submucosa， and muscularis， consistent with a granulocytic sarcoma . Immunohistochemistry showed that the neoplastic cells were positive for the expression of lysozyme， CD68， CD33， and HLA-DR . Subsets of the malignant cells were also positive for the expression of CD117， myeloperoxidase， and CD56， but negative for CD34， consistent with acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML M5)

【14】Discussion

【15】Granulocytic sarcoma， or chloroma， are both terms used to describe an extramedullary tumor occurring in soft tissue or bone with the presence of atypical myeloid or monocytic blast cells . Granulocytic sarcomas are extramedullary manifes-tations of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The term 'chloroma'was first used in 1853 and refers to the sometimes green col-oration of the tumor . The t(8；21) karyotype is associated with AML solid tumors ， but was not identified in this case. Granulocytic sarcoma may present as a sign of leukemic re-lapse in patients who have been previously diagnosed with AML， or who may not have received prior therapy， or as a de novo diagnosis in the absence of any previous pathology .

【16】Granulocytic sarcoma at any site is a rare occurrence， with a reported incidence of between 2.5-9.1% in patients with pre-existing AML . Granulocytic sarcoma usually occurs in the bone， skin， and lymph nodes . The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is an extremely rare anatomical site for the involvement of granulocytic sarcoma. Due to this rarity， the exact frequency of involvement of the Gl tract is relatively unknown， as there have been few previously reported cases of Gl granulocytic sarcoma. One of these cases involved the small intestine， mes-entery， and mesenteric lymph nodes in a 25-year-old man . Another case report was that of a 64-year-old woman with known AML who was diagnosed with a granulocytic sarcoma of the gallbladder， 20 days after receiving chemotherapy . These previous case reports highlight the two distinctive fea-tures of the present case report， the rare anatomical location in the gallbladder， and the de novo diagnosis.

【17】Patient symptomatology in any Gl-based granulocytic sarcoma may vary and is based on location. In this case report， the patient presented with acute cholecystitis and cholangitis. A temporal and causal relationship between the patient's clinical presentation and granulocytic sarcoma could only be established once histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirmed the presence of atypical myelomonocytic blasts in the gallbladder. In the French-American-British (FAB) classifi-cation system of hematologic disease， the presence of mono-cytic blasts demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in the cell infiltrates of the gallbladder wall confirmed the diagnosis of granulocytic sarcoma or extramedullary acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML M5) . Further clinical studies are required to determine the optimal treatment modalities specifically for GI-based granulocytic sarcoma.

【18】Conclusions

【19】This report is of a case of an exceedingly rare presentation of a hematologic malignancy， granulocytic sarcoma， or ex-tramedullary acute myeloid leukemia (AML)， also known as chloroma， in the gallbladder. A combined diagnostic strategy， including imaging， endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancrea-tography (ERCP)， histopathology，immunohistochemistry， and laboratory investigations were required to confirm the diag-nosis of granulocytic sarcoma of the gallbladder. Timely diag-nosis is essential， so that appropriate treatment with chemo-therapy can begin as soon as possible， as granulocytic sarcoma has a high mortality rate.

【0】Background：

【1】Cerebral air embolism is a rare iatrogenic complication of endoscopic procedures that can result in irreversible neurological damage. The symptoms of cerebral air embolism are nonspecific and may be attributed to seda-tion-related complications and central nervous system insults. Having awareness of this rare iatrogenic event and deciding on immediate imaging when it is suspected are essential for prompt diagnosis and treatment.

【2】Case Report：

【3】A 72-year-old man with a past medical history of alcoholic liver cirrhosis with associated portal hypertension underwent an outpatient esophago-gastroduodenoscopy for surveillance of esophageal varices. During the pro-cedure， the patient retched several times and developed a mucosal tear， which was repaired using endoscopic clips. After the procedure， the patient remained sedated for a prolonged time and was subsequently unrespon-sive. Nonenhanced CT of the head showed several foci of gas throughout the subarachnoid spaces. Follow-up nonenhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated ischemic changes， which were more promi-nent along the right cerebral hemisphere.

【4】Conclusions：

【5】Cerebral air embolism is an iatrogenic complication of endoscopic procedures that can result in irreversible neu-rological damage. It must be included in the differential diagnosis of a patient presenting with altered mental status and neurological deficits after an endoscopic procedure. Diagnostic imaging can be useful in identifying key features of this iatrogenic event. Timely diagnosis and treatment can improve patient outcomes.

【6】MeSH Keywords： Embolism， Air· Endoscopy， Gastrointestinal · latrogenic Disease· Stroke Cerebral air embolism is a rare iatrogenic complication of en-doscopic procedures that can result in irreversible neurologi-cal damage. Endoscopic procedures require pressurized air in sufflation， which can facilitate the introduction of air into the vascular system . Most cases of cerebral air embolism are associated with disruption in the mucosa， which consequently exposes the vasculature to pressurized air， and in severe cas-es it may lead to hemodynamic instability or ischemia of end organs， such as the central nervous system. The symptoms of cerebral air embolism are nonspecific and may be attributed to sedation-related complications and central nervous system in-sults， such as ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke . Therefore， cerebral air embolism must be suspected in patients present-ing with neurologic symptoms after an endoscopic procedure to conduct prompt diagnosis and treatment. We present a case of an esophago-gastroduodenoscopy procedure complicated by a Mallory-Weiss tear that resulted in cerebral air embolism.

【7】Case Report

【8】A 72-year-old man with a past medical history of alcoholic liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension underwent esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy for surveillance of esophageal varices. Midazolam was administered for conscious sedation. He retched sever-al times during the procedure and bleeding was noted at the esophagogastric junction， which was associated with a small mucosal tear. The patient was subsequently treated using en-doscopic clips and epinephrine injection. Air insufflation of the lumen was needed to allow adequate visualization for repair. After the procedure， the patient remained somnolent and un-responsive for a prolonged period. He was endotracheally in-tubated and transferred to our institution.

【9】When the patient arrived at our institution， approximately2 hours after the event， his Glasgow coma scale was eye re-sponse， 1；verbal response， not testable； and motor response，3. Right-sided myoclonus was identified. The cranial nerve exam was remarkable for absent pupillary response， bilateral-ly. The deep tendon reflexes were normal (2+)， bilaterally. The patient's blood pressure was 153/69 mmHg (MAP： 97)； pulse，90 beats per min； and oxygen saturation， 100% (on mechan-ical ventilation).

【10】The noncontrast-enhanced head computed tomography (CT) scan performed the day of admission demonstrated multiple foci of gas throughout the subarachnoid spaces of the right cerebral hemisphere . Given the patient's CT findings and clinical history， the main diagnostic consideration was iat-rogenic cerebral air embolism. We quickly started him on hy-perbaric oxygen therapy and the antiepileptic drug levetirace-tam to treat involuntary movements， which were suggestive of anoxic myoclonus.

【11】Follow-up noncontrast brain magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) was performed the next day (1 day after admission)， demonstrating gyriform cortical restricted diffusion through-out the right cerebral hemisphere and， to a lesser extent， through the left frontal， parietal， and occipital lobes . Corresponding fluid-attenuated inversion-recovery (FLAIR) hy-perintensity and edema throughout the aforementioned re-gions of restricted diffusion was detected . In addi-tion， regions of white matter edema were seen throughout the supratentorial compartment， which were more extensive in the right cerebral hemisphere. Foci of susceptibility artifacts throughout the right cerebral hemisphere were visualized， cor-relating with air emboli which were better visualized on the previous head CT scan . The main cerebral arterial and venous sinus flow voids were preserved.

【12】The patient received 48 h of hyperbaric oxygen therapy， with no neurological improvement. A noncontrast-enhanced head CT performed on admission day 3 demonstrated loss of the gray-white matter differentiation involving the entire right hemisphere， left frontal and parietal upper convexities， and left occipital lobes， correlating with hypoxic-ischemic injury and brain edema in these regions .

【13】The patient remained in the intensive care unit for 5 weeks， showing no neurological improvement. Prognosis was discussed with the family and the case was taken to the ethics commit-tee. The family decided to sign do-not-resuscitate and do-not-intubate orders， and the patient underwent withdrawal of life support. He was discharged 1 week later to a nursing home to continue comfort care measures.

【14】Discussion

【15】latrogenic air emboli during endoscopic procedures are rare， difficult to diagnose， and have a high potential for being se-vere and fatal. An air embolism develops when air is intro-duced into the vascular system and can be facilitated with a pressurized air source . A disruption of the mucosal bar-rier is commonly associated in such cases . Prompt recog-nition of neurologic symptoms after an endoscopic procedure is imperative to reduce mortality .

【16】Most air embolism cases are associated with endoscopic ret-rograde cholangiopancreatography， but this iatrogenic event has also been described in several endoscopic procedures such as colonoscopy and esophago-gastroduodenoscopy， as in the case of our patient . The present case suggests that the esophago-gastroduodenoscopy procedure performed for gastric varices surveillance provoked severe retching that led to the mucosal tear and bleeding， which occurred during the proce-dure. Already dilated， tortuous， and fragile varices put the pa-tient at an increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding be-cause of his chronic liver disease. Furthermore， the increase in intra-abdominal pressure from retching， along with the added insufflation pressure for better visualization of the tear， pro-duced the pressure gradient necessary to introduce air into the venous circulation. According to the literature，the hypo-thetical volume of air needed to cause fatal air embolism is around 3-5 mL/kg or a high rate of infusion of 300-500 mL at100 mL/sec . Patients may present with sudden respiratory distress due to decreased gas exchange at the capillary bed of the lungs ， one of the mechanisms associated with arterial air emboli. Other pathophysiologic events described in the lit-erature include right-to-left shunting associated with a patent foramen ovale， which accounts for 10% to 40% of cases .

【17】Without causal distinction， it is understood that all arterial air emboli result in direct ischemic consequences in end organs due to the vasospastic effects of flow obstruction， which are caused by microbubbles in the arterial system . The micro-bubbles can also induce platelet aggregation， endothelial dys-function， disruption of the blood-brain barrier， and brain ede-ma . In the case of our patient， the neurological deterioration， which was evident with a Glasgow coma scale of 4， was highly suggestive that the passage of air into the arterial system led to a cerebral air embolism and consequently the acute isch-emia of different brain regions. Given that the brain is highly dependent on oxygen to meet its energy demands， an arteri-al air embolus can result in failure to meet this requirement， resulting in severe irreversible damage， which highlights the urgency of making a proper diagnosis .

【18】The ability to identify the clinical presentation of cerebral air embolism is crucial to having the high clinical suspicion need-ed to provide appropriate preventive measures while waiting for a definitive diagnosis， thereby minimizing delay in treat-ment. Donepudi et al. described 41 cases of cerebral air embo-li associated with endoscopic procedures that presented with nonspecific neurological symptoms including altered mental status， prolonged sedation after anesthesia， and cerebral ede-ma . Similarly， our patient presented with many of these symptoms， which can be easily confused with a cerebrovas-cular accident or sedative effects， making diagnosis difficult to attain simply by clinical presentation. This case highlights the importance of attaining rapid diagnostic imaging in such a clinically challenging presentation that demands emergent action and advises the cautious use of sedative therapy while performing such procedures in high-risk patients.

【19】If air embolism is suspected， various steps may improve pa-tient outcomes， such as stopping the use of pressurized air， hyperventilation on 100% oxygen， and placement of patient in the left lateral decubitus and Trendelenburg (head below feet) positions . Head CT imaging is emergent once pro-cedural or post procedural neurological symptoms become apparent， with or without cardiorespiratory instability， in an at-risk patient. Some authors suggest bedside echocardiogra-phy as a safer alternative modality as it can decrease the de-lay in diagnosis and prompt immediate therapeutic interven-tion . A head CT scan is highly sensitive to air emboli when it is done in a rapid time frame； when the CT is delayed， air can be quickly absorbed from the vasculature and diagnosis can be missed . Most air emboli have been detectable since the American College of Radiology (ACR) established that CT scanners must be able to acquire images with a minimum slice thickness of 2 mm or less . However， the acquisition slice thickness varies depending on institutions'protocols. The ACR recommends an acquisition slice thickness no larger than5 mm . Some authors suggest that if the CT scan fails to detect the macroscopic air bubbles， diffusion-weighted MRI can be obtained to show early ischemic changes， which are apparent in less than 20 minutes 9.

【20】On noncontrast head CT， a cerebral air embolism is diagnosed by identifying serpiginous air densities throughout the sub-arachnoid spaces and parenchyma. The air densities can be identified at venous or arterial structures， so it is always im-portant to examine the venous sinuses and the course of the main cerebral arteries. Arterial and venous air emboli usual-ly affect the frontal and parietal lobes. However， it has been described that in arterial air emboli， punctate air emboli can be found in the brain parenchyma， trapped in arterial capil-laries . Most patients with a clinical suspicion of ischemic stroke require a noncontrast brain MRI. Most stroke proto-col MRI includes T1-weighted， T2-weighted， FLAIR， diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)， and susceptibility-weighted imaging(SWI). DWI is the most important sequence because it reveals early ischemic changes with a sensitivity of 90% and specifici-ty of 97% . SWl is a sequence used to detect hemorrhage. However， it is well known that air can be a magnetic suscep tibility source， resulting in a blooming artifact. This blooming artifact is particularly helpful in detecting microbubbles， as in our case . Additional findings related to ischemic changes include edema， which produces high signal intensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR images.

【21】In the case of our patient， emergent noncontrast-enhanced CT imaging supported the clinical suspicion that cerebral air em-boli occurred during the esophago-gastroduodenoscopy pro-cedure. The imaging demonstrated multiple gas foci through-out the subarachnoid spaces of the right cerebral hemisphere， which correlated with the brain MRI done a day later. Once clinical suspicion is supported by imaging， treatment should not be delayed. Our patient was quickly started on hyperbar-ic oxygen therapy， which decreases morbidity and mortali-ty in patients if given within 24-30 h， preferably . The treatment consists of 100% oxygen at above sea lev-el pressure with a target arterial oxygen level higher than2000 mmHg .Hyperbaric oxygen acts by compressing and diffusing air bubbles to decrease the ischemic period and pro-vide oxygenation to the hypoxic tissues through high arterial oxygen concentrations . This therapy has demonstrated a reduction in mortality from higher than 90% in untreated patients to 7% in patients receiving hyperbaric oxygen thera-py . However， researchers estimate that if the embolus is larger than 50 mL， treatment may be ineffective .

【22】Our patient's neurological status was severely affected even after hyperbaric oxygen treatment， and the patient was lat-er discharged for hospice care with a poor prognosis. We can hypothesize that air emboli volume was too large for the hy-perbaric therapy to be effective. Similarly， Eoh et al. presented a case report of iatrogenic air embolism after upper endosco-py in a patient with no mucosal tears prior to the procedure that was treated immediately with hyperbaric oxygen. As in our case， the patient showed no improvement in neurologi-cal status， and a post-treatment head CT scan showed a large right cerebral hemispheric infarction， which also resulted in hospice care.

【23】A cerebral air embolism can cause detrimental and irreversibly catastrophic damage in a patient’s neurological function. A re-cent retrospective study reported that the case fatality rate of air embolism is 15.4%， and that the risk ofinpatient mortality was much higher in patients with comorbidities . Our pa-tient presented with a previous history of alcoholic cirrhosis， portal hypertension， and esophageal varices， which increased his risk for such a diagnosis and for a poor outcome after treat-ment， when compared to other patients with no comorbidi-ties. The literature also showed that air emboli is an indepen-dent predictor of mortality ， which is why early diagnostic imaging is crucial to identify the cause of potential mortality in these patients and accelerate treatment to alleviate the ex-tent of nonreversible neurological damage， although the major-ity of patients can persist with some neurological deficits .

【24】Bai et al. described the case of a patient with liver cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C infection who presented with hemateme-sis and underwent an endoscopic variceal ligation. During the procedure， the patient had a generalized convulsion and be-came hemodynamically unstable. The patient died 1 day later in the intensive care unit. Although this patient did not receive hyperbaric oxygen therapy， the case highlights the possible impact in fatality rate due to underlying comorbidities .

【25】In the case of our patient， an esophago-gastroduodenosco-py procedure for gastric varices surveillance was complicated by iatrogenic air emboli， which could have been easily over-looked in medical practice. However， this case reinforces the idea that cerebral air emboli can happen during an endoscopic procedure and must be suspected in a patient presenting with sudden changes in cognition or neurological deficits during or after the procedure. Additionally， sedation in high-risk patients should be used with caution， and patients should be followed post procedure with serial neurological tests to avoid miss-ing clinical signs that could lead to immediate diagnostic im-aging and prompt treatment with hyperbaric oxygen to im-prove patient outcome.

【26】Cerebral air embolism is a rare iatrogenic complication of en-doscopic procedures that can result in a fatal outcome. It must be suspected in patients presenting with altered mental sta tus and neurological deficits after an endoscopic procedure. Since clinical presentation can be nonspecific， diagnostic im-aging should be a priority early on in order to identify the key features of this iatrogenic event. Timely diagnosis and treat-ment can improve patient outcome.

【0】ABSTRACT This case report follows a right-handed 26-year-old female with a past medical history of schizoaffective disorder， patellofemoral syndrome， De Quervain’s tendonitis， and remote foot surgery with acute onset debilitating foot pain from an initial presentation at an urgent care facility to her eventual return to work. Special attention is drawn to physical exam findings， natural history， differential diagnosis， clinical pearls， and details on the legal responsibility of physicians. This case study hopes to provide a framework for how physicians and other providers can help patients as they navigate the harsh realities of the healthcare system and provide some key clinical pearls to ensure that the patient is kept front and center in the minds of those providing the necessary healthcare for the patient’s psychiatric， social，and physical needs.

【1】KEYWORDS Orthopaedics， Bruised Bone， Patient-Centered Care， Diagnostic Work Up

【2】Introduction

【3】Care for a patient's needs often means more than just caring for their physical health. Social， financial， transportation， psy-chological， and other forms of suffering often prevent proper recovery for their physical conditions. These needs can be ad-dressed with support from an interdisciplinary team through proper evaluation， careful interviewing， and discussion. This case study looks at a patient with increasing foot pain，causing her to miss work and struggle with her own needs. Throughout the case study， special attention is brought to the patient's psy-chological and financial needs and how these were either met or not met by her providers. Emphasis on patient-centred care and further recommendations for ensuring the best quality of care for patients are discussed， along with the pathophysiology and the differential diagnosis of bone contusions.

【4】The patient is a right-handed 26-year-old female with a past med-ical history of schizoaffective disorder managed with lithium and aripiprazole， patellofemoral syndrome now resolved， De Quervain's tendonitis now resolved， and remote foot surgery to correct congenital pes planus. The patient presents to an urgent care facility with right foot pain that appeared while waking. This pain has interrupted her ability to ambulate at her manual labour job and in her small studio apartment. She states that this injury has become worse over the last three days. The level of injury，according to the patient， has interrupted her ability to cook for herself， leading to an increase in prepared(frozen/microwavable) meals as her only source of nutrition. It has also led to the patient being unable to properly shower due to pain elicited while standing. Her statement is，“When I'm at home，I'm in bed." The patient states that she has only mildly increased her level of exertion at work due to a promo-tion and that this pain started roughly one week after increasing her exertion at work. She states that the pain is located on the dorsal lateral portion of the foot. She describes the pain as a mild stabbing pain (2/10) when she is resting， which becomes much worse when she stands or ambulates (6 or 7/10). She denies any numbness or tingling and states that the pain remains in the same area without radiation. She states that she had been utilizing over-the-counter dosages of ibuprofen (up to 1200 mg) and acetaminophen (4000 mg per day)， which she stated was the maximum she had looked up for use. During this visit， no imaging studies， laboratory studies， or other diagnostic tools were utilized. On physical examination， the patient was febrile at 100.5°F and demonstrated some weakness with ambulation on the right foot. There was guarding of the right foot with ambulation due to pain， and the patient refused to put her full weight on the right foot. There was no erythema， nor was her foot warm to the touch. There was some minor swelling of the right foot， but it was not firm and did not demonstrate any pitting with palpation. With both soft and deep palpation of the lateral metatarsal region， the patient demonstrated pain and wincing， which she stated was a 6/10 pain. There was a normal passive and active range of motion with 5/5 strength in both the plantar flexors and dorsiflexors. The Achilles reflex was 2+， and the Babinski reflex was downgoing and normal. The remainder of the physical examination was within normal limits.

【5】Differential Diagnosis

【6】Based on the patient’s history and physical examination， there is a set of major etiologies which could have caused the patient's symptoms. These are modulated considering the context of her previous foot surgery increased work efforts， and her fever. First and foremost， the most important diagnosis to consider and rule out regarding the fever and intolerance to use is septic arthritis . While the patient had a fever， her symptoms and the physical examination make this an unlikely cause . The second worrisome diagnosis that must be ruled out is nerve compression， as seen with tarsal tunnel syndrome. While this diagnosis is another major cause of foot pain that should be considered， it does not match the patient's history or physical examination and should be ruled out. The location of the pain， the lack of typical pain characteristics， and the timeline all made this diagnosis less likely.

【7】Once these potential major damaging causes of foot pain were considered less likely， the remaining potential causes of her foot pain under consideration were musculoskeletal. These include peroneal tendonitis， a stress fracture， bruised bone， and plantar fasciitis. Because the pain was not in the heel or the bottom of the foot， plantar fasciitis was considered a less likely cause. The remaining diagnosis of peroneal tendonitis， bone contusion， or stress fracture was considered the most likely cause. The patient was encouraged to see her primary care physician if the pain did not resolve.

【8】The Story Continues

【9】The patient was given a temporary or working diagnosis of peroneal tendonitis and encouraged to see her primary care physician if the pain did not resolve. During this visit， the patient was not given a note or excuse for work. She was told to follow up if it got worse. She stated that no further education was provided during this initial encounter. Over the following weekend， the pain increased in severity and the patient set up an appointment with her primary care physician as soon as she could be seen. At the primary care office， the patient was told that the pain seemed too great for simple tendonitis and was instructed to get an X-ray. The patient scheduled her X-ray for the earliest available time： a week from her initial primary care appointment. Before leaving her primary care office， the patient was given a walking boot for the foot and was told to use this any time she was ambulating. The patient was not given a work accommodation note explaining the medical need for the boot before leaving the office. She was told to follow up if it got worse. Again， she stated that no further education was provided during this initial encounter. When her workplace demanded documentation to comply with OSHA requirements， the patient called the office requesting documentation. This phone call and subsequent phone calls to the office requesting said documentation were either not responded to， or the patient was told they would send it to her shortly， which never occurred. Due to the lack of OSHA-compliant paperwork， the patient had to work on the injured foot or take time off. During this time， the patient took a day off from work to get the X-ray， which her primary care physician ordered， but she did not hear back from the office. After roughly one and a half weeks of intense symptoms， the patient’s pain levels eventually became so great that she presented to the emergency room. The foot X-ray she had received three days prior in the emergency room was read. No abnormalities were found on the foot X-ray . She was sent home and instructed to set up an outpatient appointment with orthopaedics. Again， no doctor's note or accommodation note for the patient’s work was provided. This lack of documentation led to further injury of the affected foot as the patient felt inclined to continue work， and the patient’s baseline depressive symptoms became increasingly worse.

【10】The patient's increased depression symptoms included hav-ing a newly acquired fear of not receiving adequate treatment， thoughts of suicidal ideation (all passive with further probing)， and increased anxiety into her condition and its clinical nature. She stated that she began to fear that the pain and difficulty with ambulation were “all in her head". Finally， she feared that her family and friends might begin to discount her suffering and that she felt trapped between the actual pain and the lack of knowledge and treatment. Following the patient’s visits to the Urgent care and ER， she had a delay in care for roughly two weeks. She was given a diagnosis and treatment plan upon seeing the orthopaedic surgeon.

【11】Final Diagnosis and Treatment

【12】Based on the lack of evidence of infection， the lack of imag-ing findings， the history， and the physical examination， the or-thopaedic care team stated that this was most likely a bruised bone： the step in mechanical injury which precedes a stress fracture . Based on the nature and aetiology of the injury secondary to increased weight and effort placed on the actual bones， the clinical team recommended that the patient take some time off from her manual labour job. The orthopaedic surgeon stated that， like a sprained joint or a strained muscle， only rest， ice， compression， elevation， and time are necessary. Finally， he stated that if the pain did not subside within six weeks of the use of the walking boot that she should schedule a return visit to consider the next steps. At the end of the encounter， the patient stated that she had struggled to get paperwork filled out by other providers so that she could either have accommodations or take a short medical leave of absence. She requested that the orthopaedic surgeon fill out her short-term disability paperwork so that she could take some time off from work to recover.

【13】Discussion

【14】The end diagnosis of the patient revealed that they were suffer-ing from a bone contusion or bruised bone. These particular injuries are believed to be from microtrauma to the trabecular network within the bone of interest . These microtraumatic in-juries lead to medullary oedema and some micro-haemorrhage and inflammation in the local area， which are not easily vis-ible with radiographic imaging modalities such as plain film X-rays . The major sub-injury types are subchondral lesion， interosseous bruising， and subperiosteal hematoma； a bone con-tusion comprises one or more of these subtypes of injuries The mechanism by which this microtrauma can oc-cur varies from patient to patient， but the most common cause of bone contusion is that of acutely increased utilization. It is also often seen with acute traumatic injuries where the bone is damaged or damaged secondary to other injuries sustained during the traumatic event 4，5，6J. Because of the microtrau-matic mechanism of injury， the imaging modality of choice is magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). On a T1 imaging modality， there is often a focal area of hypointense bone marrow. On a T2 fat-saturated image， the same focal area of hypointense bone marrow is often seen. The imaging findings for the traumatic injury take up to 48 hours to be visible on MRI and often can remain for up to six months. Because of the often-limited re-sources or access to MRI imaging in outpatient settings， a bone contusion can be diagnosed clinically as a diagnosis of exclusion. The diagnostic criterion for the clinical diagnosis includes ruling out other major diagnoses and a negative plain film x-ray .

【15】First to Care， Then Do No Harm

【16】In the patient's case， there were several instances where discus-sion with the patient or preparation for the patient's needs (i.e. writing a doctor's excuse) would have prevented the patient from further harm. While not often brought to the forefront of patient care， ensuring that the patient has documentation available to them for work purposes is often necessary to ensure that they can rest and recover from injury or illness. Without ensuring that the patient has access to the necessary paperwork as seen in this case study， the patient might be required to either take time off from work or work through the injury or illness. Much of the time， especially with patients like that in this case study， this time off may not be paid， especially without docu-mentation from a physician， which leads to a decrease in the patient's earnings for the recovery period. Common reasons why a patient might not be given a note during a physician's room visit include the provider not knowing the occupation of the patient， the provider not having a detailed enough history to understand how this might be secondary to the patient’s pre-vious foot surgeries and foot injury which could be occupation related， and finally not asking whether the patient might need to take either time off from work or have accommodations while trying to heal.

【17】Many patients， like the case study patient， often feel they must bargain for their health from a place of fear and confu-sion. This can lead to either patients being lost to follow-up or finding themselves with increased health care costs. Because of the nature of the power differential and the nature of the fear and trust that patients place in their healthcare providers， taking the additional few minutes to explain clinical reasoning and ask about the patient's needs and goals of care and incorporating these aspects into the clinical care is tantamount to proper man-agement of disease-making the patient's team members in their clinical care team .

【18】Because of the nature of the injury， the importance of home care， including heat and/or ice for pain and swelling， non-steroidal anti-inflammatories for pain， rest of the affected foot， compression of the injured foot， and finally， the elevation of the affected limb to decrease swelling should have been deployed at every visit. Instructing the patient on what they can do at home to help their pain can not only empower the patient but can also help reduce the pain and further complications. The trip to the ED could have been avoided had this been utilized in the care and education of the patient. This might also have led to a less costly course of care as the patient could have been directly referred to the orthopaedic surgeon by her PCP instead of seeing an ER physician in between her initial encounter and her visit to the surgeon's outpatient clinic.

【19】Psychiatric support and further questioning about the pa-tient's psychological needs are key. As was seen with the patient in the clinical case， she suffered from an increasing burden of psychiatric distress from her current disease state co-mingled with her already pertinent schizoaffective disorder. The patient’s illness harmed her psychological state， which needed to have been addressed to ensure that she could care for her physical suffering. In a study published in 2009， patients suffering from a musculoskeletal injury (ACL tear) reported worse rates of de-pression than those struggling with concussions or the controls. Therefore， as physicians and providers， it is key that the patient's physical， emotional， and mental needs be met simul-taneously， especially when that patient struggles to navigate a difficult-to-understand and hard-to-manage healthcare system. The average American cannot afford an unexpected $400 bill. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis' report released in the summer of 2021， roughly 50% of American fam-ilies would have great difficulty paying for a $400 emergency expense， and 19% would be unable to afford the cost whatso-ever . This becomes pertinent as unpaid time off from work can easily outpace even a $400 cost. Therefore， in caring for the entire patient and not just the disease， it is key to confirm that disability paperwork， doctor’s notes， and other pertinent paperwork are filled out promptly to ensure that the patient's psychosocial needs are met.

【20】Lastly， the authorial team cannot stress enough the impor-tance of patient education. The patient in the case report had already previously had foot surgery. Because of the nature of her work and the potential for re-injury， it is key that providers provide highly salient and useful clinically relevant resources on how to prevent reinjury of the affected foot. This can include information on stretching exercises， hot and cold compresses to place on the affected previously injured foot， instructions on the utilization of KT tape or Ace wrap to support the musculoskele-tal injury， and lastly， referrals to Physical therapy as necessary to ensure that the patient had access to therapeutic exercises for their own personal benefit and long-term health .

【21】Conclusion：

【22】This case study looked over the diagnostic workup of a patient by her primary care physician and the perils and pitfalls of a disconnected healthcare system. Throughout the workup of the patient's foot pain， there were several instances where consid-ering the patient's specific social needs would have prevented further harm or injury. Therefore， it is the authorial team's great-est recommendation that a proper needs assessment be taken， including biological，psychological， and social factors that might affect the patient's health and needs during their recovery from illness； and that in each case， these specific needs be brought under consideration and treated as is seen in the best interest of the patient.

【0】ABSTRACT Complete situs inversus is a congenital condition which involves the complete transposition of all thoracic and abdominal organs. This condition poses a technically challenging issue for the procedure of transcatheter pulmonary vein isolation to treat atrial fibrillation. We have recently experienced one case of situs inversus complicated with cardiac tamponade after successful ablation. The patient is a 67-year-old woman with a history of situs inversus totalis. She presented to our emergency department with repeated episodes of drug-resistant paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Ra-diofrequency ablation was preferred. During the procedure， we performed interatrial septal puncture under intracardiac ultrasound guidance and isolation of all four pulmonary veins was achieved. Ten minutes after removing the sheaths from left atrium， the patient developed cardiac tamponade and prompt pericardiocentesis was needed. Pericardial effusion resolved on the next day and she was discharged three days later. No recurrence of atrial fibrillation has been documented after the procedure. Judging from clinical progress， pericardial effusion is speculated to occur after removal of the sheath.

【1】KEYWORDS Situs inversus， Atrial fibrillation， Cardiac Tamponade， Catheter ablation

【2】Introduction

【3】Dextrocardia with situs inversus is a rare cardiac positional5C0anomaly which involves complete transposition (right to left reversal) of all thoracic and abdominal organs. It is estimated to occur in 2 per 10 000 live births. The heart， in particular， lies towards the right thoracic cavity (dextrocardia). Catheter abla-tion in these particular patients poses a great challenge in terms of spatial orientation and manipulation of the catheters. We have recently performed pulmonary vein isolation for drug-resistant paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) in a patient with situs inver-sus with a successful outcome. Unfortunately， a complication of cardiac tamponade occurred after removal of the sheaths.

【4】A 67-year-old Japanese woman with a history of situs inversus totalis and rheumatoid arthritis presented to our emergency department with repeated episodes palpitations. Her electro-cardiogram (ECG) showed tachycardia caused by AF. Two an-tiarrhythmic drugs failed， and cardioversions were required to convert the rhythm to sinus rhythm. Catheter ablation was cho-sen as a preferred option to treat this drug-resistant paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

【5】We did a preoperative contrast CT to evaluate the orientation of each structure of the heart . Under general anaesthesia， we performed septal puncture with an RF needle (Baylis Med-ical， Montreal， Canada) shaped in a deeply acute angle from right IC under intracardiac ultrasound guidance. After several attempts and reshaping of the needle， we successfully punctured interatrial septum and advanced three sheaths to anatomical left atrium. Radiofrequency ablation of 4 pulmonary veins was per-formed . Successful Electrical isolation of four pulmonary veins was achieved. Ten minutes after removing the sheaths from the left atrium， the patient developed cardiac tamponade and prompt pericardiocentesis was performed. Pericardial ef- fusion resolved on the next day and she was discharged three days later. No AF episodes have been documented after the procedure.

【6】Discussion

【7】Pulmonary vein isolation(PVI) by catheter ablation is currently regarded as a gold standard for drug-resistant AF treatment. Inpatient with situs inversus， the procedure is feasible but more complicated with potentially higher rates of compli-cation. There have been several case reports of successful PVI in patients with situs inversus totalis and dextrocardia using radiofrequency， cryoballoon， magnetic and robotic navigation with no complications. To our knowledge， this is the first case report of cardiac tamponade after the procedure.

【8】The first step to approach functional left atrium involves atrial septal puncture. This step is generally done using a needle under the fluoroscopic guide. The sudden movement of the tip of the needle when it falls into fossa ovalis is a good indicator for site selection. Tenting of interatrial septum under contrast injection and pressure record connected to the lumen inside the needle are also frequently used during puncture.

【9】Trans-septal puncture in patients with situs inversus and dex-trocardia is considered to be the most challenging step during ablation. The orientation of interatrial septum concerning infe-rior vena cava (TVC) is reversed and the window for puncture can be strikingly narrow as showed in preoperative CT scan in this case.

【10】Pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade are a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of this procedure. The incidence of cardiac tamponade ranges between 0.2% and 5%. in PVI done in a patient with normal anatomy. The incidence might be higher in patients with situs inversus.

【11】In order to avoid such complications， we used intracardiac echo and RF needle. However， in this case， even after extreme bending of the tip of the needle， it could not reach the ideal thinnest part of the atrial septum. Puncture could only be done at a relatively thick part of the septum.

【12】During the procedural time of 2 hours of PVI， vital signs were stable and there was no enlargement of the cardiac silhouette on fluoroscopy. However， when PVI was completed and transsep-tal sheaths were removed， blood pressure dropped rapidly to80/50 within 10 minutes. Based on timing and the speed of accumulation of pericardial effusion， we speculate that bleed-ing occurred through the puncture site. The puncture was not properly done at the thinnest part of fossa ovalis but probably through interatrial connective tissue space. After removal of the sheaths， bleeding rapidly occurs through this hole through which three 8.5Fr-sheth were placed causing cardiac tamponade. However， spontaneous hemostasis was achieved after reversal of anticoagulation because blood clot slowly builds up in peri-cardial space causing elevation of pressure that surpasses left atrial pressure.

【13】Manipulation of ablation catheter inside functional left atrium was done using contact force-sensing catheter under3D electroanatomical mapping and fluoroscopic guidance. Con-tact force was around 5-20 grams， and PVI was achieved without many difficulties. We thus consider that the chance of cardiac perforation occurred during this process of ablation is probably IOW.

【14】Conclusion

【15】Pulmonary vein isolation in patients with situs inversus and dextrocardia is feasible and has a favourable outcome but the procedure may be technically challenging. Careful selection of the septal puncture site is crucially important. Otherwise， complications such as cardiac tamponade might occur. Prepro-cedural CT and intraoperative intraprocedural intracardiac echo guidance can help in visualization and locating the optimal puncture site at fossa ovalis. 3D mapping facilitates anatomical understanding and can reduce operation and fluoroscopic time during the ablation process.

【16】Abbreviations

【17】PVI： pulmonary vein isolation； AF： atrial fibrillation； CT： com-puted tomography； IC： inferior vena cava.

【0】Background：

【1】Mixed adenoneuroendocrine carcinoma of the gallbladder (gMANEC) is an extremely rare cancer. Most of the cases are reported in Asia， North America， and Europe， with no cases reported in Latin America； this is the first report for this region， and the 24h case reported worldwide.

【2】Case Report： A 68-year-old woman was referred to our department due to asthenia and moderate abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant for 6 months， with imaging examinations showing a solid heterogeneous expansive lesion in gallbladder topography and segment lV of the liver. The MRI displayed an expansive and heterogeneous lesion with inaccurate limits in the gallbladder affecting segment lVb of the liver， in addition to lymphadenopathy in the hepatic hilum. A cholecystectomy with resection of segments IV-B and V of the liver (radical cholecystecto-my) and hepatic hilar lymphadenectomy were performed.Anatomopathological examination and immunohisto-chemistry confirmed a primary mixed adenoneuroendocrine carcinoma of the gallbladder. The patient received adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy； however， after the patient reported experiencing low back pain， a CT was performed， revealing retroperitoneal metastasis， and the radiotherapy was interrupted. Currently， the patient has a stable disease， following a protocol of 5-Fluorouracil and somatostatin， and she reports having low back pain of low intensity.

【3】Conclusions：

【4】This is the 24h gMANEC case reported in the literature. The tumor was successfully resected； however， the pa-tient presented retroperitoneal metastasis 6 months after surgery， despite combined adjuvant therapy.

【5】Keywords： Carcinoma·Gallbladder Neoplasms· Mixed Tumor， Malignant·Neuroendocrine Tumors (HC/UFPE)， Recife， PE， Bra zil3 General Surgery Division， Hospital das Clinicas at Federal University of Pernambuco (HC/UFPE)， Recife， PE， Brazil4 Medical School， Federal University of PernambucO (UFPE)， Recife， PE， Brazil5 Pathology Division， Napoleao Laureano Hospital， Joao Pessoa， PB，Brazil6 Department of Surgery Federal University of Pemambuco (UFPE)， Recife， PE， Brazil Papillary adenocarcinoma is the most common neoplasm of the gallbladder， accounting for about 98% of all cases， while critical neuroendocrine tumors account for only 0.5% of all neoplasms of this organ . In 2019， the WHO classification of digestive system tumors classified the neoplasms composed of neuroen-docrine and non-neuro endocrine components as mixed neu-roendocrine non-neuroendocrine neoplasms (MINENs).Mixed adenoneuroendocrine carcinomas (MANEC) are an aggressive subtype of MINENJ.

【6】MANECs are even more difficult to diagnose as a primary tu-0as mor of the gallbladder. MANECs belong to a specific group of tumors that exhibit great heterogeneity， given that the per-centages of adenocarcinomatous and neuroendocrine differen-tiation can vary according to their classification. To define the presence of MANEC， at least 30% of each tumor component must be determined . In most cases， this tumor appears in the colon， appendix， rectum， or stomach， and is rarely found in the biliary tract， pancreas， or gallbladder .

【7】Clinical symptoms of mixed adenoneuroendocrine carcinoma of the gallbladder (gMANEC) are nonspecific， such as epigastric or right hypochondrium pain， nausea， and vomiting . However， asymptomatic cases are also reported . These factors con-tribute to a late diagnosis， which worsens the prognosis and survival rates. The low number of reported cases limits the ac-knowledgement of primary gMANEC as a possible diagnosis.

【8】Herein， we report a case of primary gMANEC， the first reported in Latin America and the 24th worldwide . This case has been reported in line with the SCARE criteria.

【9】Case Report

【10】In August 2019， a 68-year-old woman was referred to the Surgical Oncology Division at the Napoleao Laureano Hospital in Joao Pessoa， Brazil， presenting with abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen and asthenia for 6 months， without associated weight loss， nausea， vomiting， or altera-tions in either urinary or intestinal habits. The laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasonography (US) ev-idenced a solid， well-defined， hyperechogenic lesion with well-defined limits in segment Ⅳ of the liver， measuring 4.1x3.8 cm.

【11】In our center， we perform the investigation with an abdom-inal computed tomography (CT)， which evidenced a slight-ly hypodense and heterogeneous expansive lesion， measur-ing 4.0x3.9 cm， with heterogeneous contrast enhancement in the topography of segment Ⅳ of the liver. The referred le-sion was also extending to the gallbladder site， presenting no cleavage plane with this organ. The gallbladder was partially filled with amorphous content， most likely due to a gallstone. There were no signs of dilation of intra- or extrahepatic bile ducts .

【12】To obtain more details for a possible surgical intervention， a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed， reveal-ing an infiltrative and heterogeneous lesion in the gallblad-der， measuring approximately 8.8x5.7 cm. Moreover， the le sion presented imprecise limits and a heterogeneous signal in the T1-  and T2-weighted  sequences， with hypovascular contrast enhancement， affect-ing segment lb of the liver. In addition， lymph node enlarge-ment in the hepatic hilum was also detected . To stage the neoplasm， a chest CT was performed and no altera-tions were evidenced. Due to the preoperative diagnosis of a gallbladder tumor， an exploratory laparotomy was indicated with a proposal for a radical cholecystectomy.

【13】Surgical Findings and Anatomopathological Examination

【14】During the surgery， an extensive tumor in the gallbladder was observed， extending to segments IV and V of the liver， as de-scribed in the preoperative imaging exams. Explorations of the cystic and common bile ducts were performed and no signs of neoplastic invasion were found. Lymph node enlargement was observed in the hepatic hilum； however， there were no signs of peritoneal spread or other organ metastasis. A chole-cystectomy associated with resection of segments I-B and V of the liver and lymphadenectomy of the hepatic hilum were performed. The postoperative course was uneventful and the patient was discharged on the 6th postoperative day.

【15】The excised gallbladder and liver segments together measured13.0x10.0x9.0 cm. The gallbladder presented a smooth and brownish external surface and greenish rough mucosa. A vege tating lesion measuring 2.0x1.0 cm was detected. Furthermore， there was a bloody area on the gallbladder surface，measur-ing 19.0x7.0 cm， firmly adhered to the liver.

【16】The cuts revealed a brownish lesion， sometimes firm-elastic， sometimes friable， involving the gallbladder wall and liver pa-renchyma， measuring 9.0x4.0 cm. Microscopical examination showed an intestinal morphology pattern along with extensive solid areas with poorly differentiated histological grade (G3). Two of the 3 lymph nodes removed presented neoplastic in-vasion. There was also a perforation in the visceral peritoneal， with neoplastic infiltration in the adjacent liver segment and intratumoral coagulative necrosis. The surgical margin had no evidence of neoplastic involvement. Therefore， the patholog-ical staging was TNM： pT3 pN1MO/IIIB.

【17】Histopathology evidenced 2 morphological components，one with neuroendocrine differentiation and the other with poor-ly differentiated adenocarcinomatous component . The immunohistochemical (IHC) study of the tumor cells was positive for the following markers： CK7 (SP52)， CK20 (SP33) in foci， Synaptophysin (SynA)， and chromogranin A (CgA)， CDX2 (AMT 28)， and the proliferation index Ki-67 was 90%. Therefore， a mixed adenoneuroendocrine carci-noma of the gallbladder (gMANEC) was confirmed.

【18】The patient has been followed up by clinical oncology with the initial proposal of adjuvant treatment with 10 chemo-therapy sessions with 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) and radiotherapy. Initially， the oncology team opted not to prescribe somatosta-tin analogs due to the absence of symptoms related to neu-roendocrine neoplasm. However， 6 months after surgery， the patient started reporting persistent low back pain of moder-ate intensity. A CT was then performed， revealing retroperito-neal metastasis， evidenced by multiple lymph nodes enlarge-ment in para-aortic， retrocaval， and precaval locations at the level of the pancreas head . Therefore， radio-therapy was interrupted and somatostatin analogs were start-ed. Currently， 3 months later， the patient has stable disease， with mild back pain.

【19】Discussion

【20】The majority of the literature on gMANEC consists of case re-ports and small case series， all from Asia (67%)， North America， and Europe. Moreover， to date， only 23 cases had been de-scribed， and none were from Latin America . To date， including data from the present study， the mean age of pa-tients with gMANEC is 61 years and the sex ratio is 5： 19(male： female).

【21】As mentioned above， the clinical features of gMANEC are non-specific . A recent systematic review， published in 2019， showed that the majority of them (60%) presented epigastric or right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain， whereas 40% were asymp-tomatic at diagnosis . Furthermore， MANECs can be classified as functional or non-functional depending on the hormone syn-thesis and endocrine syndrome inductions， although only 3.3% presented syndromes involving hormone production  and most of the patients do not present carcinoid syndrome .

【22】Besides these nonspecific clinical features， imaging examina-tions also show low accuracy in this diagnostic process， which highlights the importance of the postoperative histopatholog ical examination in confirming the diagnosis . Moreover， frequently， only a single histological component of the tumor is identified， which impairs the diagnosis and treatment pro-cesses . Therefore， chromogranin A (CgA) and synaptophy-sin (SynA) markers are of paramount importance， given their high sensitivity for MANECs diagnosis， being present in up to92.3% of patients 4.

【23】The World Health Organization (WHO) Grading for Neuroendocrine Tumor establishes 3 degrees of tumor differ-entiation： G1 (mitotic count <2 per 10 HPF and/or a Ki-67 in-dex <2%)； G2 (mitotic count 2-20 per 10 HPF and/or Ki-67 in-dex of 3-20%)； and G3 (mitotic count >20 per 10 HPF and/or Ki-67 index>20%) . NETs classified as G1 or G2 are asso-ciated with a better prognosis than the NETs of other histo-logical subtypes . In our case， the neuroendocrine portion presented a Ki-67 index of 90%， which would make it a neu-roendocrine neoplasm of third grade or low differentiation ac-cording to the WHO classification . Moreover， the ade-nocarcinoma portion was also classified as Grade 3； therefore， a poor prognosis is expected.

【24】The ideal therapy is still undetermined， although the combi-nation of complete surgical resection， adjuvant chemothera-py， and the use of somatostatin seems to be the mainstay of treatment . In the majority of cases reported in the literature， the decision was made to perform a radical cholecystectomy， with segmentectomy (segments I and V) of the liver along with lymphadenectomy. Generally， it is expected that 74% of patients undergoing cholecystectomy due to a gallbladder neu-roendocrine tumor will present recurrence or metastasis； how-ever， a cholecystectomy combined with hepatic segmentecto-my and lymphadenectomy increases the 5-year survival rate from 21.3% to 60.4% in patients with this type of tumor .
